name: Renaissance humanism
scope: Renaissance humanism as the defining sources describe it: the educational and cultural movement that began in the Italian cities in the 13th–14th centuries and spread across Europe to about 1600, centred on the studia humanitatis (grammar, poetry, rhetoric, history and moral philosophy) and the Ciceronian ideal of humanitas, the full development of human virtue joined to active civic life (s1, s2, s3). Its programme is a revival of Greek and Roman antiquity as the model for education, eloquence, statecraft and morals, to reform culture and, through counsel to rulers and citizens, the state (s1, s2, s3). Founders and exponents are Petrarch and Boccaccio, Salutati, Bruni, Alberti, Valla, Pico and Manetti in Italy, and Erasmus and More in the north (s1, s2, s3, s4). The sources stress that it was not a single philosophy with a fixed set of doctrines (s3) and that its content varied by time, place and writer, from Florentine civic republicanism to courtly, Platonist and Christian strands (s3, s4); positions are taken only where a source ties them to the humanists. Excluded: the modern secular, rationalist or human-centred 'humanism' of the 20th century, which Britannica and King say the Renaissance humanists would not have recognised (s1, s3), Christian humanism as a later personalist doctrine, 'civic humanism' as a separate label, and Classical revivals elsewhere (Carolingian, 12th-century; s1). Books found only by title and not about the movement (Heidegger and the question of humanism, the Byzantine scholar Kallistos, Blayney's Age of Luther, Gragg's Latin selections) are not used as defining sources.

summary: Renaissance humanism was the educational and cultural movement, begun in Italian cities in the 13th–14th centuries and spreading across Europe, that revived Greek and Roman antiquity through the studia humanitatis (grammar, poetry, rhetoric, history, moral philosophy). Its ideal was humanitas: the full development of human virtue joined to active civic life, with eloquence as the means of guiding citizens and rulers. It was not a single philosophy, and humanists differed on politics and religion, from Florentine civic republicans to Erasmus's Christian reform, so the sources fix few positions on the test's statements.

notes: Most statements are null: King's introduction says the movement had no common set of principles on natural, social or political questions. Searched the anthology's chapters on the self, civic life, the state, religion, women and poverty, Britannica, and the key works' full texts (Pico, Praise of Folly, Valla, Alberti, Bruni) for each theme. Individual humanists took positions (Bruni on republican liberty, Valla on papal temporal power, Erasmus on peace, Vives on poor relief), but they are not shared across the movement, so they are not recorded as its answers.
